body.text: COP31 has ended with no deal on the main text. As the nearly 100,000 delegates head home from the longest climate summit to date with tales of wins, losses, and questions about the future of climate diplomacy, it’s a good time to take stock of where we are globally on climate action.

There’s no sugarcoating that the world is not doing enough to reduce emissions and avoid dangerous global warming. Current national pledges could lead to roughly 2.4 degrees Celsius of warming by 2100. That’s a significant improvement on the trajectory prior to the Paris Agreement but well off the global goal aimed at limiting dangerous warming. This will depend on nations not only delivering on existing commitments but also pushing for faster and deeper cuts to emissions.
Despite the scale of the challenge, there are reasons for hope and even optimism.

The United Nations’ 31st annual climate talks, known as COP31, have finally wrapped in Türkiye, delivering disappointment over the lack of consensus in negotiation texts, but progress in a few action agenda items. By now you will have probably already heard about the “35-by-35 Global Electrification Pledge,” to raise electricity’s share of global final energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035. While the final text fell through, around 90 countries signed on to the pledge.

Answering Brazil’s call for nations to develop plans and metrics for transitioning out of fossil fuels, five more countries, Denmark, Spain, Portugal, Luxembourg and Ireland, announced national roadmaps, joining Germany, France, Finland, the Netherlands, and the Pacific Island States.
These are important commitments. But some of the most interesting developments are happening outside of the COP process.

As nations in Asia grapple with the current fuel crisis, and brace themselves for a potential “super” El Nino, we’re seeing Governments across the region lean into climate policy in unprecedented ways.

Thailand is progressing with the nation’s first Climate Change Act, an ambitious framework that includes setting national carbon neutrality and net zero targets, emissions reporting requirements for around 4,000 big businesses, a pilot emissions trading scheme and establishing a national Climate Fund. The proposed legislation also includes the planned development of the National Emission Trading System with initial targets at high-emitting industries such as cement, metals, and petrochemicals. Clean power currently makes up less than 31 percent of Thailand’s capacity, while the current draft Power Development Plan 2026 would set the country on a path to 53 percent within the plan’s first decade. That means roughly tripling the share in about 11 years, with an aim of reaching 65-89 percent by 2050.
While the Thai Act is still to be passed by the parliament, and its details may evolve, the signal sent by the draft framework shows the scale of some of what’s happening across Asia.
South Korea is one such nation. It’s taking a different but equally significant approach.

India and China have attracted attention for their rapid renewable energy rollout, surpassing 50 percent and 60 percent of installed capacity respectively. But South Korea has upped the ante in recent weeks with a 1,000 trillion won ($747 billion) Korea Green Transformation (K-GX) strategy through to 2035. The K-GX is focused on renewables and decarbonizing heavy industry. This is no small feat given the energy demands of South Korea’s heavy industrial sector.

This new commitment complements their existing ambitious commitments in sectors such as offshore wind, where South Korea aims to create a 4GW annual pipeline of projects until they achieve 25GW by 2035. To put that in context, 90GW of offshore wind capacity is currently installed globally, with about half in China alone. If Seoul can pull that off it will be a massive achievement and show what’s possible with sufficient will and resources.
Finally, there is some good news from Uncle Sam. The midterm elections in the United States might well be viewed in hindsight as a critical turning point for climate action.

Firstly, the Democrats took back control of the U.S. Congress. The last time they controlled all three branches of the federal government under President Biden they passed the Inflation Reduction Act, which allocated $370 billion for climate action. That sort of outcome is not likely to happen again while President Donald Trump is in office, but it gives you a sense of what might happen in states that the Democrats now control. Six new states now have Democratic “trifectas” (control of both chambers of the Congress and the governorship), and many have made commitments to support renewable energy and climate action.

There is no more complex global challenge than decarbonization. Announcements don’t always result in outcomes, and outcomes aren’t always what they first seem to be. It’s time to be clear-eyed and stay focused on real-world results. But sometimes it feels like the only thing the world has more of than greenhouse gas emissions, is pessimism about climate action. We can challenge both. So let’s all take heart from the fact that good things can happen and are happening, in Asia and beyond. Every step forward counts.
